title: Bacon Mummy Meatloaf
summary: Meatloaf wrapped in a bacon lattice like a mummy, with olive eyes. Smoked low and slow.
story: The kids will not stop staring at this one — and then they'll eat half of it. A solid backyard meatloaf wrapped in a woven bacon lattice like mummy bandages, smoked until the bacon crisps and the middle hits temp. The olive eyes go on at the end. Carve it at the table for maximum effect.

items: 1/4 cup ketchup or BBQ sauce, for glazing

steps.title: Mix the loaf
steps.body: Mix the beef, breadcrumbs, eggs, onion, garlic, ketchup, Worcestershire, rub, salt, and pepper until just combined. Don't overwork it. Shape into a loaf on a foil-lined sheet pan or a grill-safe pan.

steps.title: Weave the mummy
steps.body: Lay out the bacon in a lattice over the loaf, crisscrossing like mummy bandages. Leave a small gap near one end for the face.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for 2.5 to 3 hours, until the internal temp hits 160°F. Brush with ketchup or BBQ sauce in the last 30 minutes.

steps.title: Eyes and rest
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes, then press two black olive halves into the face gap for eyes. Slice and serve.

proTips: Thin bacon crisps; thick bacon stays chewy. Go thin.
Put the loaf on a wire rack over a sheet pan so the bottom doesn't steam.

title: Smoked Bat Wings
summary: Chicken wings in a dark, sticky sweet-heat glaze. They come out looking like they flew straight out of a cave.
story: The dark rub and the sticky glaze do all the Halloween work here — these wings come off the pit almost black and shining. Sweet heat underneath, crispy-edged, gone in minutes. Make more than you think you need.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the wings dry. Toss with all the rub ingredients until evenly coated.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F for about 1.5 hours, until the wings hit 175°F internal and the skin has tightened up.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Warm the BBQ sauce, honey, and soy sauce together. Toss the wings in the glaze.

steps.title: Set the glaze
steps.body: Return to the smoker for 15 minutes so the glaze sets sticky and dark. Serve hot.

proTips: Dry wings = crispier skin. Pat them down and let them air-dry in the fridge an hour if you can.
Don't glaze too early or the sugars burn. Glaze at the end.

title: Pulled Pork Stuffed Mini Pumpkins
summary: Little pie pumpkins stuffed with pulled pork and cheddar, smoked until the pumpkin goes tender.
story: This is what you do with leftover pulled pork in October. Hollow out little pie pumpkins, pack them with pork and cheese, and let the smoker do the rest. The pumpkin steams itself tender from the inside and you can scoop it right out with the pork.

steps.title: Hollow the pumpkins
steps.body: Cut the tops off the pumpkins and scoop out the seeds and stringy guts. Sprinkle the insides lightly with salt and pepper.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Toss the pulled pork with the BBQ sauce, onion, and half the cheddar. Pack the mixture into the pumpkins and top with the rest of the cheddar. Set the tops back on, tilted like little hats.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F for about 1 hour, until the pumpkin flesh is tender when poked and the cheese is melted.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve whole — scoop the tender pumpkin right out with the pork.

proTips: Use pie pumpkins, not carving pumpkins — carving pumpkins are stringy and bland.
Any leftover smoked meat works here: brisket, chicken, turkey.

title: Smoked Hot Apple Cider
summary: A pot of spiced apple cider warmed on the smoker with a whisper of apple wood smoke.
story: While the Halloween cook runs, a pot of cider rides along on the smoker and picks up the faintest kiss of apple wood. Cinnamon, cloves, star anise, orange — the whole house smells like October. Ladle it hot straight from the pot.

steps.title: Load the pot
steps.body: Pour the cider into a cast iron Dutch oven or heavy pot. Stir in the brown sugar if using, then add the cinnamon sticks, cloves, star anise, and orange slices.

steps.title: Smoke-warm
steps.body: Set the pot on the smoker at 275°F with light apple wood for 1.5 to 2 hours, stirring once or twice, until steaming hot and spiced through.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Ladle into mugs, straining out the whole spices if you like. Keep the pot on the warm side of the pit for refills.

proTips: Light smoke only — heavy smoke turns cider bitter. Apple wood, small fire.
Tie the cloves and star anise in cheesecloth for easy fishing out.

title: Halloween Snack Mix
summary: Bold-style Chex snack mix toasted on the smoker, then tossed with candy corn and chocolate candies.
story: This one's the Bold version — extra Worcestershire, garlic, and onion, with bagel chips folded in like the real Bold blend. An hour on the smoker, then it cools down and gets the Halloween treatment with candy corn and chocolate candies. The bowl empties itself.

items: 1 cup orange and black chocolate candies

steps.title: Coat
steps.body: Toss the Chex, pretzels, bagel chips, and peanuts in a big foil pan. Drizzle with the melted butter, Worcestershire, seasoned salt, garlic powder, and onion powder; toss to coat.

steps.title: Smoke-toast
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F for 1 hour, stirring every 15 minutes, until crisp and toasted.

steps.title: Cool and candy
steps.body: Cool completely — the candy melts if the mix is warm — then fold in the candy corn and chocolate candies.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Bowl it up. Keeps a week in an airtight container, if it survives the night.

proTips: Stir every 15 minutes or the bottom pieces over-toast.
Wait until it's fully cool before the candy goes in — warm mix makes a melted mess.

title: Skillet Fried Apples
summary: Apple slices fried in a cast iron skillet with butter, brown sugar, and cinnamon until tender and glazed.
story: Kristy's request. Sliced apples cooked down in butter and brown sugar with cinnamon and nutmeg until they're tender and swimming in syrup. Serve them next to pork chops like they do down South, or over a scoop of vanilla ice cream. Either way, don't expect leftovers.

items: 5 firm apples (Golden Delicious or Granny Smith), cored and sliced

steps.title: Melt the butter
steps.body: Melt the butter in a cast iron skillet over medium heat.

steps.title: Add everything
steps.body: Add the apple slices, brown sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, salt, and the splash of apple juice. Stir to coat.

steps.title: Fry
steps.body: Cook 15 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the apples are tender and glazed in a thick syrup.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve warm — next to pork, or over ice cream.

proTips: Firm apples hold their shape; soft ones turn to mush. Golden Delicious or Granny Smith.
Don't walk away at the end — the sugar syrup can go from glazed to scorched fast.

title: Candy Apple BBQ Chicken
finish: 175°F in the thigh, 160-165°F in the breast, glaze set sticky
summary: Smoked chicken halves under a sticky apple butter glaze that sets up like a candy apple. Sweet, smoky, and shining.
story: Inspired by Lane's BBQ's candy apple chicken halves — this is our own take with Ember House Rub and a warm apple butter glaze that caramelizes right on the bird. The glaze goes on late so the sugars shine instead of burn. Cut into halves, they look like something off a Halloween candy table and eat like the best BBQ chicken you've had.

items: 2 whole chickens (3-4 lbs each), cut in half — or 4 store-bought chicken halves

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Pat the halves dry. Season all over with Ember House Rub, working some under the breast skin. Rest 30 minutes.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F over apple or cherry wood, skin-side up, until the breast reads 150°F — about 2 to 2 1/2 hours.

steps.title: Make the glaze
steps.body: Warm the apple butter, honey, apple juice, and butter in a saucepan until melted together into a smooth glaze.

steps.title: Glaze and set
steps.body: Brush the glaze thick over every half. Return to the smoker for 15 minutes so it sets.

steps.title: Finish candy-style
steps.body: Brush with Ember Finishing Glaze and give it 10 more minutes until sticky and caramelized. Thighs should read 175°F, breast 160-165°F. Rest 10 minutes and serve with extra glaze on the side.

proTips: Glaze late — the sugars in the apple butter and honey will burn if they go on too early.
Warm glaze brushes on smoother and sticks better than cold glaze straight from the jar.
Don't skip the rest. Ten minutes lets the glaze firm up into that candy shine.

title: Armadillo Eggs
summary: Jalapeños stuffed with cream cheese, wrapped in sausage and bacon, smoked until crisp. The ultimate pop-in-your-mouth BBQ bite.
story: Part jalapeño popper, part scotch egg, all barbecue. The sausage shell keeps the cheese from escaping and the bacon bastes the whole thing as it crisps. One cut open with the cheese running out will end the argument about who gets the last one.

steps.title: Prep the peppers
steps.body: Cut the tops off the jalapeños, halve lengthwise, and scrape out the seeds and membranes. Leave some membrane if you like heat. Wear gloves.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Mix the cream cheese, cheddar, and 1 Tbsp Ember House Rub. Stuff each jalapeño half full.

steps.title: Wrap in sausage
steps.body: Divide the sausage into 12 portions. Flatten each into a thin patty and wrap it completely around a stuffed half, pinching the seams shut.

steps.title: Wrap in bacon
steps.body: Dust with the rest of the rub, then wrap each one in a slice of bacon. Secure with a toothpick.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F about 2 hours, until the bacon is crisp and the sausage reads 160°F inside. Brush with Ember Finishing Glaze in the last 15 minutes if you want them sticky.

proTips: Thin bacon beats thick here — it actually crisps instead of staying chewy.
Pinch the sausage seams shut or the cheese will find its way out.
Make a double batch. They vanish.

title: Molasses Pull Taffy
finish: Hard ball stage, light tan and satiny after pulling
summary: Old-time mountain taffy pull candy — dark molasses, chewy, wrapped in wax paper twists.
story: Taffy pulls were a social event in the mountains — everybody's hands got buttered and everybody got candy. Molasses is the Appalachian sweetener, and pulled slow it turns light and satiny. This isn't barbecue, but it belongs to the same people.

items: 2 Tbsp butter, plus more for your hands

steps.title: Cook
steps.body: Combine everything except the baking soda in a heavy pot. Cook over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then stop stirring. Cook to 260°F (hard ball stage).

steps.title: Foam and pour
steps.body: Stir in the baking soda — it will foam up. Pour onto a buttered slab or sheet pan.

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Cool 10-15 minutes until you can handle it without burning yourself.

steps.title: Pull
steps.body: Butter your hands. Stretch, fold, and stretch again for 15-20 minutes until the taffy turns light tan and satiny.

steps.title: Cut and wrap
steps.body: Pull into ropes, cut with buttered scissors, and wrap each piece in wax paper twists.

proTips: A second pair of hands makes the pulling go twice as fast — that's how the old taffy pulls worked.
If it sticks to your teeth, you pulled it right.
Wrap every piece — left unwrapped, they'll melt into one big lump.

title: Black Walnut Fudge
finish: Soft ball stage, thick and matte after beating
summary: Classic chocolate fudge loaded with black walnuts — the Appalachian nut.
story: Black walnuts aren't like the English walnuts in the store — they're stronger, earthier, and they taste like the mountains. Folks used to gather them in the fall and crack them on a rock. Folded into fudge, they're the whole reason for the recipe.

steps.title: Cook
steps.body: Combine the sugar, cocoa, milk, and salt in a heavy pot. Cook over medium heat, stirring until dissolved, then stop stirring. Cook to 234°F (soft ball stage).

steps.title: Cool
steps.body: Remove from heat and drop in the butter — don't stir. Let it cool to 110°F (lukewarm to the touch).

steps.title: Beat
steps.body: Add the vanilla and beat with a wooden spoon until thick and it loses its gloss.

steps.title: Nuts and pan
steps.body: Fold in the black walnuts. Spread in a buttered 8x8 pan. Cool completely, then cut into squares.

proTips: Black walnuts are stronger than English walnuts — a cup is plenty.
Don't beat it before it cools to lukewarm or it will go grainy.
A candy thermometer is worth it here — 5 degrees off either way changes the texture.

title: Sorghum Peanut Brittle
finish: Hard crack stage, thin and glassy
summary: Peanut brittle made with Kentucky sorghum instead of corn syrup — deeper, darker, better.
story: Sorghum was the mountain sweetener — folks grew the cane and cooked the syrup down every fall. Swapping it for corn syrup in peanut brittle gives you a deeper, almost smoky sweetness. Use cocktail or Spanish peanuts — raw ones are hard to find, and these go in late so they don't scorch.

items: 1 1/2 cups cocktail peanuts or Spanish peanuts
1/4 tsp salt (skip if your peanuts are salted)

steps.title: Cook the syrup
steps.body: Combine the sugar, sorghum, and water in a heavy pot. Cook over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, to 290°F.

steps.title: Add peanuts
steps.body: Stir in the peanuts and cook to 300°F (hard crack stage), stirring so nothing scorches.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Off the heat, stir in the butter, then the baking soda and vanilla — it will foam up.

steps.title: Spread and break
steps.body: Pour onto a buttered sheet pan and spread thin. Cool completely, then break into pieces.

proTips: Have everything measured before you start — once it hits temp it moves fast.
Thin spreads snap better than thick ones.
Cocktail or Spanish peanuts go in late because they're already roasted — raw peanuts would go in much earlier.

title: Peanut Butter Potato Candy
summary: Depression-era Appalachian candy — mashed potato, powdered sugar, and peanut butter rolled into pinwheels.
story: Sounds strange until you taste it. This came out of hard times in the mountains — a potato, a bag of powdered sugar, and peanut butter turned into candy. Kelly's had it, and it eats like a peanut butter roll.

items: 1/2 cup plain mashed potato (no butter, no salt — just potato)
1 lb powdered sugar (about 4 cups), plus more for dusting

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.body: Mash the warm potato completely smooth — no lumps. Stir in the vanilla, then beat in the powdered sugar a cup at a time until it forms a stiff dough.

steps.title: Roll out
steps.body: Roll the dough on a powdered-sugar-dusted surface into a rectangle about 1/4 inch thick.

steps.title: Fill
steps.body: Spread peanut butter over the whole thing, edge to edge.

steps.title: Roll and chill
steps.body: Roll it up jelly-roll style, wrap in plastic, and chill at least an hour. Slice into pinwheels.

proTips: The dough is sticky — that's normal, just keep dusting with powdered sugar.
Chill before slicing or the pinwheels squish.
The potato must be lump-free — push it through a ricer or sieve if you have to.
